Modern.tagline: A food delivery service. Modern. Honest.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Doorbell is the moment of the food handoff — single archaic domestic word, immediately readable. Single-word naming follows the considered-modern delivery school (Caviar, Postmates of original era).
Modern.industrySummary: Modern food delivery has consolidated around three or four giants and a long tail of regional players. The customer is design-literate, increasingly tired of the platform-aesthetic sameness, and willing to pay more for a service that actually delivers the food intact.
Modern.competitorLandscape: DoorDash (doordash.com) holds the U.S. giant peer position. Uber Eats (ubereats.com) sits at the same tier. Wonder (wonder.com) does the modern verticalized middle. Grubhub (grubhub.com) is the older incumbent. We sit closer to Wonder in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A food delivery brand that competes on whether the food arrives intact.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Orders food two or three times a week. Already pays for one premium delivery service. Will switch the moment one of them ships a soggy order.

dos: Show the delivery time and the temperature on the package
Speak to the customer as a person who just paid for food
Confirm orders in one short note
donts: Photograph delivery riders against neutral backdrops

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. Doorbell in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, two thin curves suggesting rising steam, used as the favicon and on every delivery bag seal.

typography.primary: Inter for product UI and headlines
typography.secondary: IBM Plex Mono for delivery times and prices
typography.rationale: Inter handles the marketing and app. The mono carries the times and prices.

customSections.body: No loyalty-tier upsell screens. No 'extra delivery insurance' add-on. No celebrity-restaurant marketing. No 'wellness meal' bundles.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: An app that books in three taps. Each order ships with a temperature-checked seal. A monthly email if the customer hasn't ordered in a while, written like a friend asking what they're eating.

Modern.tagline: A small modern delivery service. One borough.
Modern.brandDescription: Crosstown Delivery is a modern food delivery service operating exclusively within a single urban borough, with a small list of partner restaurants and direct courier employment.
Modern.scope:
Crosstown Delivery works across:
• Food delivery within a single defined urban borough
• Small partner-restaurant list (under 100 partners)
• Direct employment of couriers with published hourly rates
• Single fixed delivery fee per order, no surge pricing
• Annual customer and partner update letter
Modern.mission: To make food delivery work for the borough — for the couriers, the partner restaurants, and the customers.
Modern.vision: A neighbourhood delivery service whose ten-year anniversary sees the same restaurants on the platform.
coreValues: Considered — the partner list is curated.
Modern — couriers are employed, not contracted.
Direct — fixed delivery fee, no surge.
Warm — the borough is the company.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Crosstown is the urban-trade phrase for travel across a borough or city center — single archaic urban-vocabulary word + plain category suffix. Stands in the lineage of considered-modern delivery services with a clear geographic focus (Caviar's original SF-only positioning, Wolt's Helsinki-led approach).
Modern.manifesto: Most food delivery platforms grow geographically as fast as possible. We started Crosstown to do the opposite — one borough, a small list of partner restaurants, couriers employed directly with published wages. The service works because everyone in the chain is treated as part of the same neighbourhood.
Modern.industrySummary: Food delivery has consolidated under a small number of global platforms (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) with broad geographic coverage. The opening underneath is for a smaller, geographically-focused service that operates with direct courier employment and a curated partner list.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Caviar (originally trycaviar.com, now within DoorDash) was the closest peer in considered urban delivery. Wolt (wolt.com) holds the considered-modern peer slot at international scale. Local Pickup (localpickup.com) plays the borough-focused peer position. Tock (exploretock.com) plays the considered-restaurant peer reference. We sit alongside Wolt with a single-borough focus and direct courier employment.
Modern.positioningStatement: Crosstown Delivery is a modern food delivery service operating within a single urban borough with a small partner-restaurant list and directly-employed couriers.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on geographic focus and operational integrity. Single borough. Curated restaurant list. Couriers employed directly. Fixed delivery fee, no surge pricing.

Care about courier wages and tipping clarity.
Avoid surge-pricing platforms.
Want a small reliable partner list.
motivations: Want a delivery service that operates well in their borough.
Want couriers paid fairly with published wages.
Want a curated list of considered restaurants.

messagingPillars.name: Direct courier employment

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words. Saturday Delivery names a specific moment in the week that has always meant something: weekend, hosting, the bigger meal. The brand puts the highest-effort meal of the week in the brand position. Distinctive, slightly old-world, and immediately understood.
Luxury.story: Saturday Delivery began as a single delivery service for the kind of household that hosts properly on Saturdays. The founders had spent years inside larger catering companies and wanted to operate on a smaller, more careful schedule. The service operates only on Saturdays. The client list is small by design.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end food delivery has been dominated by tech-platform marketplaces. There's a parallel market for high-end private delivery services that operate like a household catering arrangement. Once-a-week service, small client list, real chefs and real ingredients delivered to a household that knows how to receive them.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Goldbelly (goldbelly.com) holds the institutional gourmet delivery peer position. Caviar (trycaviar.com) sits at the premium platform tier. Tock (exploretock.com) does the design-led booking middle. We sit smaller than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A weekly private delivery service for households that host properly.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often hosts Saturday dinners. Has a regular catering arrangement they're tired of. Wants a single service that handles the food, the wine, and the timing.

dos: Address the client by surname

Send a paper card the week before

Luxury.tagline: A private culinary delivery service. By membership.
Luxury.brandDescription: The Wynward Table is a heritage private culinary delivery service operating in three cities, with a capped member roster and a small list of partner chefs producing custom meals to order.
Luxury.scope:
The Wynward Table works across:
• Private culinary delivery by membership
• Custom meal preparation by partner chefs
• Direct delivery in unmarked vehicles to member households
• Annual member dinners hosted at the partner restaurants
• Multi-generational member family relationships
Luxury.mission: To deliver chef-prepared meals to a small membership in the heritage private-chef tradition.
Luxury.vision: A culinary delivery service whose 100th member dinner is hosted in the same private rooms as the first.
coreValues: Senior — the service has operated since 1998.
Discreet — member identity and meal preferences stay private.
Considered — partner chefs are part of the practice.
Warm — multi-generational members are the practice's organising principle.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Wynward Table uses the definite-article + place-name + Table convention common to heritage private dining clubs (The Wolseley, The Ivy Club, The Garrick Club's dining room tradition). Wynward is a constructed place-name with a heritage register. The Table suffix places the brand firmly in the heritage private-dining tradition.
Luxury.manifesto: Most modern food delivery is platform-mediated, optimized for volume, and indifferent to the meal. The Wynward Table was founded in 1998 as a private culinary delivery service for households who wanted chef-prepared meals delivered without going through restaurants or platforms. Membership is capped. Most members are referred by existing members. Partner chefs have been with the service for decades.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium private culinary services are rare and dominated by individual private chefs and small concierge services. There is space for a small membership-based culinary delivery service operating in the heritage private-chef tradition with multiple partner chefs.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Heston Personalised Service (heston.com) plays the closest peer in heritage private culinary. Daily Harvest's premium tier plays the broader peer reference. The Marylebone (themarylebone.com) sits in the considered-private peer position. Quintessentially Culinary (quintessentially.com) plays the concierge-culinary reference. We belong with the small private-chef tradition translated to a membership-based service.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A heritage private culinary delivery service operating by membership in three cities with capped enrollment and partner chefs.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not extend the service. The three cities are the limit. Members are accepted by referral; partner chefs have been with the service for decades.

Minimal.vision: A delivery service whose 100th week of operation runs the same daily-menu format as week one.

Minimal.manifesto: Most food delivery is a restaurant marketplace with thousands of menu options. We made Tray because the actual best lunch and dinner decision is no decision at all — one menu, one kitchen, one fee per week. The menu changes daily; the format does not.
Minimal.industrySummary: Food delivery is overwhelmingly built around marketplace models with extensive menu choice. There is real space for a minimal service that strips the offering to a single daily menu from a single kitchen.

Literary — the writing about late-night culture is part of the brand.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The Late Plate is a phrase about the meal eaten after standard dining hours — the post-shift dinner, the late-night kitchen plate. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school (The After-Hours Co, The Twelve Plate Co). Stands in the lineage of declarative-position food brands with a clear time-of-operation creative argument.
Creative.manifesto: Most food delivery operates during standard restaurant hours and tapers off after 9pm. We started The Late Plate Co for the city after the restaurants close — the kitchen workers heading home, the night-shift hospital staff, the people working late, the people who eat at midnight. The service is open when most delivery is closed.
Creative.industrySummary: Food delivery operations taper sharply after standard dining hours. There is real space for a creative-led service that operates exclusively in late-night hours with partner restaurants and kitchens that prepare food specifically for the time.
Creative.competitorLandscape: goPuff (gopuff.com) plays the closest peer in late-night convenience delivery. UberEats and DoorDash operate 24/7 but with sharply reduced restaurant availability after 10pm. Wonder (wonder.com) plays the multi-restaurant late delivery reference. We sit further out — late-night-only, dedicated partner restaurants, dedicated couriers.
Creative.positioningStatement: The Late Plate Co is a food delivery service operating exclusively between 10pm and 3am with partner restaurants and kitchens preparing food specifically for late-night hours.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on the time of operation. Every aspect of the service — partner restaurants, courier shifts, packaging, voice — is designed for the late-night use case.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who work late shifts, eat dinner late, or want hot food delivered after standard delivery hours close.
behaviors: Work shifts that end after 10pm.
Eat dinner after 10pm regularly.
Order food in the late evening or early morning.
Want hot food rather than late-night convenience-store options.
motivations: Want a delivery service that operates after restaurants close.
Want partner restaurants preparing food for the time.
Want late-night culture treated as primary, not secondary.

dos: Lead with the operating hours.
Photograph late-night kitchens and night-shift workers.
Publish the quarterly essay on late-night urban culture.
Sign correspondence by the late-shift operations lead.
donts: No competition with standard delivery platforms during business hours.

messagingPillars.name: 10pm to 3am only
messagingPillars.description: We operate exclusively between 10pm and 3am, every night. There are no daytime deliveries.

messagingPillars.name: Late-night partner kitchens
messagingPillars.description: Partner restaurants prepare specific menus for the late-night service — food designed for the time, not leftover from earlier hours.

messagingPillars.name: Dedicated late-shift couriers
messagingPillars.description: Couriers work the late-shift hours by choice and have done so for at least six months. They are not pulled from daytime rotations.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — The Late Plate Co set in a quiet display serif with a small illustration of a lamp shining on a plate beside it. The mark feels printed on a late-night diner placemat.

colorPalette.name: Night
colorPalette.meaning: Primary — the colour of the urban night sky.

colorPalette.name: Lamp
colorPalette.meaning: Secondary — the colour of a diner lamp.

typography.primary: A quiet display serif for the wordmark and the quarterly essay.
typography.secondary: A neutral grotesque for the night menu and partner-restaurant listings.
typography.rationale: Two faces. The serif tells the story of the night; the grotesque carries the menu.
